title: DHS Proposes Ending Deference to Prior H-1B and L-1 Petition Approvals
excerpt: A proposed rule would remove the requirement that USCIS defer to earlier I-129 approvals, exposing H-1B and L-1 extensions and amendments to fresh adjudication, more evidence requests, and higher denial risk.
body:
• The Department of Homeland Security has proposed a rule that would remove the regulation requiring USCIS to generally defer to a prior eligibility decision on Form I-129 petitions involving the same parties and the same facts.
  • The proposal is scheduled for publication in the Federal Register on October 14, 2026, with public comments invited for 30 days after publication; the current deference rule stays in place unless DHS finalizes the change.
  • If finalized, H-1B and L-1 extensions and amendments could face fresh adjudication of issues USCIS already approved, raising the risk of requests for evidence and denials even when the job has not changed.
  • What this means for you: do not rely on a prior approval alone in an upcoming extension — build each filing with full evidence of eligibility, as Murthy Law Firm advises employers to do now.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has issued a proposed rule that would eliminate the regulation requiring U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) to generally defer to an earlier eligibility determination when it reviews a Form I-129, Petition for a Nonimmigrant Worker, according to Murthy Law Firm. The proposal, released on October 13, covers benefit requests filed on Form I-129, including extensions of previously approved nonimmigrant worker petitions.

Under the change, officers could still consider a prior approval, but they would not be required to begin their review by deferring to it. The proposed rule is scheduled for publication in the Federal Register on October 14, 2026.

What deference does today

Deference is the practice of giving weight to an earlier approval when the same worker seeks an extension under substantially similar circumstances. Under the current rule, USCIS generally defers to its previous favorable determination when a later petition involves the same parties and the same underlying facts, unless there was a material error in the earlier decision, a material change in circumstances, or new adverse material information.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=nrdOxkJdyjo

That starting point stops officers from re-litigating questions already examined — whether a job is a specialty occupation or the worker holds the required credentials — when nothing has changed. It does not guarantee an extension, but it makes routine renewals more predictable.

A policy that has flipped before

The deference approach dates to a 2004 USCIS policy memorandum that told officers to defer to prior approvals in extension cases with the same parties and facts. The first Trump administration rescinded that guidance in 2017, directing officers to adjudicate extensions without giving weight to earlier decisions. The Biden administration restored deference in 2021 guidance, and a broader overhaul of the H-1B regulations in 2024 then wrote the policy into federal regulations, Bloomberg Law reported, as cited by The American Bazaar.

Because deference now sits in a regulation, removing it requires formal rulemaking: a proposed rule, a comment period, and only then a possible final rule.

What would change in practice

If the rule is finalized as proposed, an extension would no longer start from the presumption that the earlier decision was correct. Each filing would effectively be adjudicated fresh, with the employer required to establish eligibility again under the applicable standards, even where the employment circumstances remain unchanged.

That shift is expected to produce more requests for evidence and a higher risk of inconsistent outcomes and denials on issues settled in a previous approval. Amendments — for example, an H-1B change of work location or duties — would face the same fresh scrutiny, and employers would face more work documenting points covered in earlier adjudications.

The proposal does not eliminate H-1B or L-1 extensions, and it does not revoke existing approvals. Its effect would depend on the final regulatory language and how USCIS applies it to pending and future petitions.

What it means for Indian workers and employers

Indian nationals make up a significant share of H-1B beneficiaries, working in technology, engineering, healthcare and other specialized occupations, and they file extensions repeatedly while waiting years in the green card queue. For that population, a less predictable extension process is not an abstract procedural change: a delayed or denied renewal can interrupt employment, travel, and long-term immigration planning.

The practical takeaway is immediate: submit full evidence of eligibility in each filing rather than rely on a prior approval alone, as Murthy advises, and start document collection early for upcoming extensions or amendments.

What happens next

This is only a proposal. The existing deference regulation remains in place unless and until DHS finalizes a change. DHS is inviting public comments for 30 days after the Federal Register publication on October 14, and the official notice will confirm the exact deadline. After the comment period, DHS may revise the proposal before issuing a final rule. Murthy Law Firm said it is reviewing the proposal and will provide further analysis as developments warrant.
